passage:
In Cape Town, Daniel's kitchen drawer was full of envelopes he hadn't opened. Most had the bank's red stripe on the front. When a new one came, he slid it under the others without looking.
"It'll sort itself out," he told Lindiwe, his flatmate, when she noticed the drawer wouldn't close. "Bonus season's coming. I'll handle it then." He said it lightly, but he switched to talking about football so fast that she stopped mid-sentence.
Last year's bonus had been smaller than promised. He knew that. He also knew that opening the envelopes would mean numbers, and numbers would mean doing something he didn't feel ready to do.
"There's a free advice centre near my work," Lindiwe said. "I could come with you." Daniel nodded at the kettle. "After payday, maybe."

qa.q: What was on the front of most of the envelopes?
qa.a: Most had the bank's red stripe on the front.

qa.q: Why does Daniel avoid opening the envelopes?
qa.a: Opening them would mean facing the numbers and having to act, which he doesn't feel ready for, so avoiding them feels safer.

qa.q: What protective step does Lindiwe offer, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She offers to go with him to a free advice centre, because qualified help and a supportive flatmate can make facing the problem less frightening.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Daniel changes the subject so fast?
qa.a: She may feel shut out and worried, since she noticed the drawer and was cut off mid-sentence.

grounding: A young man with mounting bills keeps saying it will sort itself out, because looking straight at the numbers would demand action he is not ready for.

passage:
By nine at night the office on the fourth floor was empty except for Kashish and the hum of the water cooler. It was the third late night this week. The manager had again promised that the overtime would "show in appraisals", the same line as last March.
Manjula from accounts stopped at her desk, bag on her shoulder. "You're here every night. And your salary was late in June too, na?"
"It's a phase," Kashish said. "Once the new client settles, it'll calm down." She kept her eyes on the screen.
She didn't mention the headaches, or the job alert she had deleted that morning without reading. Reading it would mean admitting this might not get better.
Manjula put a hand on the desk. "Just read one alert. That's all. Reading isn't quitting."

qa.q: What did the manager promise about the overtime?
qa.a: The manager promised the overtime would "show in appraisals", the same line as last March.

qa.q: Why did Kashish delete the job alert without reading it?
qa.a: Kashish felt afraid to read it, because reading it would mean admitting the job might not get better.

qa.q: What small step does Manjula suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Manjula suggests reading just one job alert, which lets Kashish look at the problem without having to decide everything at once.

qa.q: What might Manjula be noticing that Kashish isn't admitting?
qa.a: Manjula sees the late nights and the late salary as a pattern, and seems worried that Kashish keeps calling it a phase.

grounding: A young woman in a draining job keeps calling it a phase and avoids anything that would make her look at it straight.
